title: Move Plants by Readiness, Not the Calendar

content.overview: Seedlings, clones and vegetative plants develop at different rates. Use root establishment, plant vigor, available space and developmental state to decide when to advance the crop instead of treating a fixed number of days as a biological law.

vocabulary.definition: The period in which a plant develops functional roots and resumes stable growth after germination, rooting or transplant.
A defined condition that must be met before moving to the next stage.
A biologically distinct phase such as seedling, vegetative or reproductive growth.

sections.title: Roots and recovery matter after propagation
sections.body: A clone or seedling should be assessed for establishment and growth rather than moved solely because the planned date arrived.

sections.title: Plant biology sets the stage
sections.body: Vegetative and reproductive development have different structural and environmental demands.

sections.title: Available space is part of readiness
sections.body: A healthy plant can still be poorly timed if the next space is not clean, stable or available.

workedExamples: A clone with weak rooting may need more establishment time even if another clone from the same tray is ready.
A vigorous plant can outgrow a small space if flowering transition is delayed without a canopy plan.
commonMistakes: Using one age target for every genotype.
Transplanting stressed material to keep a schedule.
Advancing before the next environment is ready.
content.practicalApplication: Define simple readiness checks for rooting, transplant, training/space and flowering transition and note them in the grow log.
content.summary: Calendar dates are planning tools; biological readiness determines when plants should actually advance.
